↩ ◇ Note. The trespass offering. The Philistine priests prescribe a classic ANE healing-by-image practice: replicate the affliction in precious metal and send it back with the offending object as a placation offering. Identical reasoning underlies medieval ex-voto images (a wax leg offered to a saint for a healed leg) and recurs across early-modern folk healing traditions. The narrative is not endorsing the practice — Yahweh has not requested it — but recording the Philistines’ best guess at how to stop the plague using their own theological framework. The number five corresponds to the five Philistine city-states (Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Gath, Ekron — the traditional Pentapolis listed at 6:17), the canonical political configuration of the Philistine confederacy.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: HEMORRHOIDS, KIRJATH-JEARIM, LORD, MIRACLES, MOUSE.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MOUSE Hebrews ‘akhbar, “swift digger”), properly the dormouse, the field-mouse (1 Samuel 6:4). In Leviticus 11:29, Isaiah 66:17 this word is used generically, and includes the jerboa (Mus jaculus), rat, hamster (Cricetus), which, though declared to be unclean animals, were eaten by the Arabs, and are still eaten by the Bedouins. It is said that no fewer than twenty-three species of this group (‘akhbar=Arab. ferah) of animals inhabit Palestine. God “laid waste” the people of Ashdod by the terrible visitation of field-mice, which are like locusts in their destructive effects (1 Samuel 6:4, 11, 18). Herodotus, the Greek historian, accounts for the destruction of the army of Sennacherib (2 Kings 19:35) by saying that in the night thousands of mice invaded the camp and gnawed through the bow-strings, quivers, and shields, and thus left the Assyrians helpless. (See SENNACHERIB.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HARNESS (1.) Hebrews ‘asar, “to bind;” hence the act of fastening animals to a cart (1 Samuel 6:7, 10; Jeremiah 46:4, etc.). (2.) An Old English word for “armour;” Hebrews neshek (2 Chronicles 9:24). (3.) Hebrews shiryan, a coat of mail (1 Kings 22:34; 2 Chronicles 18:33; rendered “breastplate” in Isaiah 59:17). (4.) The children of Israel passed out of Egypt “harnessed” (Exodus 13:18), i.e., in an orderly manner, and as if to meet a foe. The word so rendered is probably a derivative from Hebrew hamesh (i.e., “five”), and may denote that they went up in five divisions, viz., the van, centre, two wings, and rear-guard.

↩ ✧ Variant. The Beth Shemesh slaughter. The MT’s "fifty thousand and seventy" is widely regarded as textually corrupt — Beth Shemesh was a small village, and 50,070 deaths there is implausible on demographic grounds and inconsistent with the smaller numbers throughout the surrounding narrative. The LXX, Josephus (Antiquities 6.16), and several Hebrew manuscripts read seventy alone (or "seventy men, fifty out of one thousand") — most modern critical editions and translations (NRSV, NABRE) restore "seventy." The verse is one of the standard textbook examples of OT numerical-textual corruption, and most scholars treat the larger figure as a scribal accretion. The theological point — that even Israelites are vulnerable to the Ark’s holiness when treated incautiously — does not require the implausible number.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ABINADAB father of nobleness; i.e., “noble.” (1.) A Levite of Kirjath-jearim, in whose house the ark of the covenant was deposited after having been brought back from the land of the Philistines (1 Samuel 7:1). It remained there twenty years, till it was at length removed by David (1 Samuel 7:1,2; 1 Chronicles 13:7). (2.) The second of the eight sons of Jesse (1 Samuel 16:8). He was with Saul in the campaign against the Philistines in which Goliath was slain (1 Samuel 17:13). (3.) One of Saul’s sons, who peristed with his father in the battle of Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:2; 1 Chronicles 10:2). (4.) One of Solomon’s officers, who “provided victuals for the king and his household.” He presided, for this purpose, over the district of Dor (1 Kings 4:11).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). UZZAH strength, a son of Abinadab, in whose house the men of Kirjath-jearim placed the ark when it was brought back from the land of the Philistines (1 Samuel 7:1). He with his brother Ahio drove the cart on which the ark was placed when David sought to bring it up to Jerusalem. When the oxen stumbled, Uzzah, in direct violation of the divine law (Numbers 4:15), put forth his hand to steady the ark, and was immediately smitten unto death. The place where this occurred was henceforth called Perez-uzzah (1 Chronicles 13:11). David on this feared to proceed further, and placed the ark in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite (2 Samuel 6:2-11; 1 Chronicles 13:6-13).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). JUDGES , BOOK OF is so called because it contains the history of the deliverance and government of Israel by the men who bore the title of the “judges.” The book of Ruth originally formed part of this book, but about A.D. 450 it was separated from it and placed in the Hebrew scriptures immediately after the Song of Solomon. The book contains, (1.) An introduction (1-3:6), connecting it with the previous narrative in Joshua, as a “link in the chain of books.” (2.) The history of the thirteen judges (3:7-16:31) in the following order: FIRST PERIOD (3:7-ch. 5) Years I. Servitude under Chushan-rishathaim of Mesopotamia 8 1. OTHNIEL delivers Israel, rest 40 II. Servitude under Eglon of Moab: Ammon, Amalek 18 2. EHUD’S deliverance, rest 80 3. SHAMGAR Unknown. III. Servitude under Jabin of Hazor in Canaan 20 4. DEBORAH and, 5. BARAK 40 —— 206 SECOND PERIOD (6-10:5) IV. Servitude under Midian, Amalek, and children of the east 7 6. GIDEON 40 ABIMELECH, Gideon’s son, reigns as king over Israel 3 7. TOLA 23 8. JAIR 22 —— 95 THIRD PERIOD (10:6-CH. 12) V. Servitude under Ammonites with the Philistines 18 9. JEPHTHAH 6 10. IBZAN 7 11. ELON 10 12. ABDON 8 —— 49 FOURTH PERIOD (13-16) VI. Seritude under Philistines 40 13. SAMSON 20 —— 60 In all 410 Samson’s exploits probably synchronize with the period immediately preceding the national repentance and reformation under Samuel (1 Samuel 7:2-6). After Samson came Eli, who was both high priest and judge. He directed the civil and religious affairs of the people for forty years, at the close of which the Philistines again invaded the land and oppressed it for twenty years. Samuel was raised up to deliver the people from this oppression, and he judged Israel for some twelve years, when the direction of affairs fell into the hands of Saul, who was anointed king. If Eli and Samuel are included, there were then fifteen judges. But the chronology of this whole period is uncertain. (3.) The historic section of the book is followed by an appendix (17-21), which has no formal connection with that which goes before. It records (a) the conquest (17, 18) of Laish by a portion of the tribe of Dan; and (b) the almost total extinction of the tribe of Benjamin by the other tribes, in consequence of their assisting the men of Gibeah (19-21). This section properly belongs to the period only a few years after the death of Joshua. It shows the religious and moral degeneracy of the people. The author of this book was most probably Samuel. The internal evidence both of the first sixteen chapters and of the appendix warrants this conclusion. It was probably composed during Saul’s reign, or at the very beginning of David’s. The words in 18:30,31, imply that it was written after the taking of the ark by the Philistines, and after it was set up at Nob (1 Samuel 21). In David’s reign the ark was at Gibeon (1 Chronicles 16:39)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). EBEN-EZER stone of help, the memorial stone set up by Samuel to commemorate the divine assistance to Israel in their great battle against the Philistines, whom they totally routed (1 Samuel 7:7-12) at Aphek, in the neighbourhood of Mizpeh, in Benjamin, near the western entrance of the pass of Beth-horon. On this very battle-field, twenty years before, the Philistines routed the Israelites, “and slew of the army in the field about four thousand men” (4:1,2; here, and at 5:1, called “Eben-ezer” by anticipation). In this extremity the Israelites fetched the ark out of Shiloh and carried it into their camp. The Philistines a second time immediately attacked them, and smote them with a very great slaughter, “for there fell of Israel thirty thousand footmen. And the ark of God was taken” (1 Samuel 4:10). And now in the same place the Philistines are vanquished, and the memorial stone is erected by Samuel (q.v.). The spot where the stone was erected was somewhere “between Mizpeh and Shen.” Some have identified it with the modern Beit Iksa, a conspicuous and prominent position, apparently answering all the necessary conditions; others with Dier Aban, 3 miles east of ‘Ain Shems.

↩ ◇ Note. "Stone of help." Even-ha-‘ezer ("stone of the help") names the place by what it means — the gesture continues the patriarchal tradition of memorial-naming (Gen 28:18–22 Bethel, Gen 31:48 Galeed, Josh 4:8–9 Jordan stones, Josh 24:26–27 Shechem). Samuel’s formula — "Yahweh helped us until now" — is theologically precise: the past tense covers the deliverance just achieved, the "until now" leaves the future open. The verse generated one of the most enduring devotional phrases in English-language hymnody through "Come, Thou Fount of Every Blessing" ("here I raise mine Ebenezer"). The narrative also closes a frame opened in 4:1 — Israel had been defeated at the original "Ebenezer," near Aphek; now a new Ebenezer marks reversal.

↩ ◇ Note. The editorial summary. The verse functions as a Deuteronomistic closure formula on the Samuel-as-judge narrative: Samuel’s tenure is recapitulated as a period of Philistine subjugation, structurally paralleling the periods of rest under earlier judges (Judg 3:11, 30; 5:31; 8:28). The claim sits in tension with the rest of the book — Saul’s entire reign is dominated by Philistine pressure, and ch 13 will already show them deeply embedded in the hill country. The contradiction is not a failure of the editor but a marker of two competing presentations of Samuel’s era stitched together: the more idealized "rest under Samuel" tradition and the more politically realistic "Philistine ascendancy" tradition that the rest of the book preserves. The seam is one of the clearer cases of the Deuteronomistic theology imposing itself on older material.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Seer / prophet (ro’eh / nabi’). The narrator’s rare gloss on lexical change. Ro’eh ("seer," from ra’ah, "to see") is the older title, emphasizing visionary perception; nabi’ (cognate with Akkadian nabu, "to call/name") is the term that becomes standard, emphasizing the prophet as one called by, or who calls in the name of, the deity. The shift in vocabulary tracks a shift in role — from local diviner consulted for fees (cf. 9:7–8, the question of payment) to the institutional prophetic figure who delivers Yahweh’s word independently of solicitation. By the time of the writing prophets (Amos, Hosea), nabi’ has displaced ro’eh almost entirely. The gloss tells us the editor is writing well after the linguistic transition is complete.

It is afterwards applied to Zadok, Gad, etc. (2 Samuel 15:27; 24:11; 1 Chronicles 9:22; 25:5; 2 Chronicles 9:29; Amos 7:12; Micah 3:7). The “sayings of the seers” (2 Chronicles 33:18, 19) is rendered in the Revised Version “the history of Hozai” (marg., the seers; so the LXX.), of whom, however, nothing is known. (See PROPHET.)

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Nagid (נָגִיד). Yahweh tells Samuel to anoint Saul not as melek ("king") but as nagid — "prince," "leader," or "designate." The choice of vocabulary is precise: nagid is a Yahweh-designated office that does not carry the political-religious freight of melek, the term the people themselves used in 8:5 ("a king like all the nations"). The narrative thereby preserves the Deuteronomistic theological tension: the people demand a melek; Yahweh designates a nagid. The same vocabulary recurs at 10:1 (Saul anointed nagid), 13:14 (David designated nagid), and 25:30 (David future nagid). Only later does the title melek attach unproblematically. The terminology preserves the OT’s ambivalence about kingship inside the very narrative of its founding.

↩ ◇ Note. The smallest tribe. Saul’s self-deprecating reply is more pointed than humility-formula: Benjamin had been all but exterminated in Judg 19–21, the closing horror of the Judges era — only six hundred men survived the inter-tribal civil war that followed the Levite’s concubine episode. Israel’s first king is drawn from the tribe Israel itself had nearly wiped out a generation earlier. The narrative irony is heavy: monarchy emerges from the wound of the prior era, and Saul’s rule will end in another civil war between tribes. The pattern of choosing leaders from the marginal — younger sons, smaller tribes, women, foreigners — is the OT’s recurrent preference, and Saul’s case is one of its starkest. The choice also anticipates Paul’s own self-identification as "of the tribe of Benjamin" (Phil 3:5, Rom 11:1) centuries later.

↩ ◇ Note. The judge-Spirit. The phrase tzalḥah ruaḥ Elohim ("the Spirit of God rushed upon him") is the standard formula for the empowerment of judges — used of Othniel (Judg 3:10), Gideon (Judg 6:34), Jephthah (Judg 11:29), Samson (Judg 14:6, 19; 15:14). Saul is here cast as the last judge, and the Ammonite crisis as the last judge-deliverance, before the office formally transitions into kingship at 11:14–15. The same Spirit will later "depart" from Saul (16:14), with the result that an "evil spirit from Yahweh" troubles him — one of the OT’s most theologically uncomfortable passages, which the narrative places in deliberate parallel-and-inversion with this initial endowment. Saul’s tragedy is structurally framed by the Spirit’s coming and its withdrawal.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Rûwach (רוּחַ). wind; by resemblance breath, i.e. a sensible (or even violent) exhalation; figuratively, life, anger, unsubstantiality; by extension, a region of the sky; by resemblance spirit, but only of a rational being (including its expression and functions).

↩ ◇ Note. The dismembered oxen. Saul’s gesture is a deliberate echo — and reversal — of Judg 19:29, where the Levite cut his concubine’s body into twelve pieces and sent the parts through Israel as a summons to inter-tribal action. The earlier mustering produced a civil war that nearly destroyed Benjamin; Saul, the Benjamite, repeats the gesture but with oxen rather than human remains, summoning Israel to defend a city (Jabesh-Gilead) that had ironically supplied the wives that saved Benjamin from extinction (Judg 21:8–14). The literary pattern is intricate: Saul’s first kingly act re-stages the trauma of Benjamin’s near-annihilation in a saving rather than fratricidal mode. The narrator is showing the reader, before any verdict on Saul’s reign is rendered, that he begins inside a long-running tribal memory.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BEDAN one of the judges of Israel (1 Samuel 12:11). It is uncertain who he was. Some suppose that Barak is meant, others Samson, but most probably this is a contracted form of Abdon (Judges 12:13).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ZEBAH man-killer, or sacrifice, one of the two kings who led the vast host of the Midianites who invaded the land of Israel, and over whom Gideon gained a great and decisive victory (Judges 8). Zebah and Zalmunna had succeeded in escaping across the Jordan with a remnant of the Midianite host, but were overtaken at Karkor, probably in the Hauran, and routed by Gideon. The kings were taken alive and brought back across the Jordan; and confessing that they had personally taken part in the slaughter of Gideon’s brothers, they were put to death (comp. 1 Samuel 12:11; Isaiah 10:26; Psalm 83:11).

↩ ◇ Note. The conditional kingship. Samuel’s farewell address frames the new monarchy in conditional Deuteronomic terms: kingship will be a blessing if king and people remain faithful, a curse otherwise. The verse anticipates the Deuteronomistic theology of 1–2 Kings, where every king is evaluated against this standard, and the exile is read as the consequence of cumulative failure. Politically, Samuel surrenders direct judge-leadership while preserving prophetic oversight — the prophetic office now functions as the standing critique of the throne, a structure that runs from Samuel through Nathan, Elijah, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. The institutional arrangement Samuel inaugurates here will outlive the monarchy itself.

↩ ◇ Note. The intercessor. Samuel formulates intercession as obligation: ceasing to pray for the people would itself be sin. The articulation places Samuel in the line of Mosaic intercessors (Exod 32:11–14, 32:32; Num 14:13–19; Deut 9:25–29), and his self-identification with that role is explicit at Jer 15:1, where Yahweh tells Jeremiah that "though Moses and Samuel stood before me," the present generation’s judgment cannot be averted. The verse becomes a foundational text for the prophetic theology of intercession, and the Christian pastoral tradition draws on it for the duty of clergy to pray for their congregations even at personal cost. The model is striking: intercession is not optional kindness but covenantal responsibility.

↩ ◇ Note. Jonathan’s theology of warfare. Jonathan articulates the foundational principle of Israelite holy-war theology: numerical odds are theologically irrelevant when Yahweh fights. The same principle drives Gideon’s reduction from 32,000 to 300 (Judg 7), David’s confrontation with Goliath (1 Sam 17:47), and the prayer at Mizpah (2 Chr 14:11). The contrast with his father is sharp: Saul, in 13:12, sacrificed prematurely from anxiety about troop numbers; Jonathan launches a two-man assault on a Philistine garrison from the same theology Saul could not hold. The chapter is partly a study in father-and-son contrast — Jonathan emerges as the Saul who might have been, and the narrative argument for his unfitness for the throne is undercut precisely by his fitness as a man of faith.

Hebrews netsib, a prefect, superintendent; hence a military post (1 Samuel 10:5; 13:3, 4; 2 Samuel 8:6). ↩ ◇ Note. Saul’s rash oath. Saul’s curse-by-fast is the OT’s third major rash-oath text, alongside Jephthah’s vow (Judg 11:30–40) and Israel’s sworn refusal to give wives to Benjamin (Judg 21:1–7). The pattern reveals Israel’s evolving juridical understanding of unbinding rash vows: Jephthah’s vow appears to be carried out (with the daughter unredeemed); the Benjamite oath is circumvented through the kidnapping at Shiloh; here, Saul’s oath would have killed Jonathan but the people redeem him by their counter-oath (14:45). Lev 5:4 will eventually codify the redemption of unwitting oaths through guilt-offering. The verse displays a king whose theological imagination runs to curses while his son’s runs to faith — and the army votes with its feet.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ADJURATION a solemn appeal whereby one person imposes on another the obligation of speaking or acting as if under an oath (1 Samuel 14:24; Joshua 6:26; 1 Kings 22:16). We have in the New Testament a striking example of this (Matthew 26:63; Mark 5:7), where the high priest calls upon Christ to avow his true character. It would seem that in such a case the person so adjured could not refuse to give an answer. The word “adjure”, i.e., cause to swear is used with reference to the casting out of demons (Acts 19:13).

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: HONEY.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HONEY (1.) Hebrews ya’ar, occurs only 1 Samuel 14:25, 27, 29; Cant. 5:1, where it denotes the honey of bees. Properly the word signifies a forest or copse, and refers to honey found in woods. (2.) Nopheth, honey that drops (Psalm 19:10; Proverbs 5:3; Cant. 4:11). (3.) Debash denotes bee-honey (Judges 14:8); but also frequently a vegetable honey distilled from trees (Genesis 43:11; Ezekiel 27:17). In these passages it may probably mean “dibs,” or syrup of grapes, i.e., the juice of ripe grapes boiled down to one-third of its bulk. (4.) Tsuph, the cells of the honey-comb full of honey (Proverbs 16:24; Psalm 19:10). (5.) “Wild honey” (Matthew 3:4) may have been the vegetable honey distilled from trees, but rather was honey stored by bees in rocks or in trees (Deuteronomy 32:13; Psalm 81:16; 1 Samuel 14:25-29). Canaan was a “land flowing with milk and honey” (Exodus 3:8). Milk and honey were among the chief dainties in the earlier ages, as they are now among the Bedawin; and butter and honey are also mentioned among articles of food (Isaiah 7:15). The ancients used honey instead of sugar (Psalm 119:103; Proverbs 24:13); but when taken in great quantities it caused nausea, a fact referred to in Proverbs 25:16, 17 to inculcate moderation in pleasures. Honey and milk also are put for sweet discourse (Cant. 4:11).

↩ ◇ Note. Popular nullification of the king’s oath. The people’s refusal to let Saul execute Jonathan is one of the OT’s rare instances of public override of royal command. The phrase "not one hair of his head" becomes proverbial (cf. 2 Sam 14:11, 1 Kgs 1:52, Acts 27:34) — a formal idiom of total preservation. The political stake is high: the army recognizes that Jonathan, not Saul, secured the day’s victory ("he has worked with God today"), and they treat this as morally outweighing the king’s sworn word. The episode foreshadows the larger pattern in which Saul’s personal commitments will be repeatedly overridden — by Samuel (15), by Yahweh (16), eventually by his own family’s loyalty to David (18–20). The throne is formally his and functionally compromised already.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PIPE (1 Samuel 10:5; 1 Kings 1:40; Isaiah 5:12; 30:29). The Hebrew word halil, so rendered, means “bored through,” and is the name given to various kinds of wind instruments, as the fife, flute, Pan-pipes, etc. In Amos 6:5 this word is rendered “instrument of music.” This instrument is mentioned also in the New Testament (Matthew 11:17; 1 Corinthians 14:7). It is still used in Palestine, and is, as in ancient times, made of different materials, as reed, copper, bronze, etc.

↩ ◇ Note. The proverb’s first occurrence. The phrase appears here for the first time, immediately after Saul’s anointing, framing his ecstatic seizure positively as confirmation that the Spirit has fallen on him. The proverb returns at 19:24, where the same phrase frames a scene of public humiliation — Saul stripping naked at Naioth — in deliberate inversion. The two appearances bookend Saul’s reign: the proverb is born in his vindication and resurfaces in his unraveling. The phenomenon itself (group prophetic ecstasy, often with music — cf. 10:5) is well-attested in the Levantine prophetic tradition, with parallels at Mari and in the Wen-Amon report; the OT preserves it not as embarrassing primitivism but as a normal mode of Spirit activity through the period of Samuel and Saul, recurring in 19:18–24 and developing into the more interior prophetic tradition of the writing prophets.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GIBEAH a hill or hill-town, “of Benjamin” (1 Samuel 13:15), better known as “Gibeah of Saul” (11:4; Isaiah 10:29). It was here that the terrible outrage was committed on the Levite’s concubine which led to the almost utter extirpation of the tribe of Benjamin (Judges 19; 20), only six hundred men surviving after a succession of disastrous battles. This was the birthplace of Saul, and continued to be his residence after he became king (1 Samuel 10:26; 11:4; 15:34). It was reckoned among the ancient sanctuaries of Palestine (10:26; 15:34; 23:19; 26:1; 2 Samuel 21:6-10), and hence it is called “Gibeah of God” (1 Samuel 10:5, R.V. marg.). It has been identified with the modern Tell el-Ful (i.e., “hill of the bean”), about 3 miles north of Jerusalem.

↩ ◇ Note. The Philistine iron monopoly. The verse preserves a precise piece of Iron Age I political-economic information: the Philistines maintained a metallurgical monopoly that prevented Israelites from manufacturing their own weapons, forcing them to depend on Philistine smiths even for agricultural tools (13:20–21, with sharpening fees set at exorbitant rates). Archaeological work in Philistine sites (Ashkelon, Ekron, Gath) has confirmed a measurable Philistine technological lead in iron-working in this period (so Lawrence Stager and others). The detail explains why Saul and Jonathan have swords (13:22) when no other Israelite does — they are royal exceptions — and underwrites the David-and-Goliath narrative of ch 17, where David’s use of a sling (a non-Philistine weapon) inverts the technological asymmetry. The verse is one of the OT’s most concrete windows on the material conditions of pre-monarchic Israel.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). LAVER (Hebrews kiyor), a “basin” for boiling in, a “pan” for cooking (1 Samuel 2:14), a “fire-pan” or hearth (Zechariah 12:6), the sacred wash-bowl of the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 30:18, 28; 31:9; 35:16; 38:8; 39:39; 40:7, 11, 30, etc.), a basin for the water used by the priests in their ablutions. That which was originally used in the tabernacle was of brass (rather copper; Hebrews nihsheth), made from the metal mirrors the women brought out of Egypt (Exodus 38:8). It contained water where with LAVER the priests washed their hands and feet when they entered the tabernacle (40:32). It stood in the court between the altar and the door of the tabernacle (30:19, 21). In the temple there were ten lavers used for the sacrifices, and the molten sea for the ablutions of the priests (2 Chronicles 4:6). The position and uses of these are described 1 Kings 7:23-39; 2 Chronicles 4:6. The “molten sea” was made of copper, taken from Tibhath and Chun, cities of Hadarezer, king of Zobah (1 Chronicles 18:8; 1 Kings 7:23-26). No lavers are mentioned in the second temple.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HAEMORRHOIDS or Emerods, bleeding piles known to the ancient Romans as mariscae, but more probably malignant boils of an infectious and fatal character. With this loathsome and infectious disease the men of Ashdod were smitten by the hand of the Lord. This calamity they attributed to the presence of the ark in their midst, and therefore they removed it to Gath (1 Samuel 5:6-8). But the same consequences followed from its presence in Gath, and therefore they had it removed to Ekron, 11 miles distant. The Ekronites were afflicted with the same dreadful malady, but more severely; and a panic seizing the people, they demanded that the ark should be sent back to the land of Israel (9-12; 6:1-9).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PARABLE (Gr. parabole), a placing beside; a comparison; equivalent to the Hebrews mashal, a similitude. In the Old Testament this is used to denote (1) a proverb (1 Samuel 10:12; 24:13; 2 Chronicles 7:20), (2) a prophetic utterance (Numbers 23:7; Ezekiel 20:49), (3) an enigmatic saying (Psalm 78:2; Proverbs 1:6). In the New Testament, (1) a proverb (Mark 7:17; Luke 4:23), (2) a typical emblem (Hebrews 9:9; 11:19), (3) a similitude or allegory (Matthew 15:15; 24:32; Mark 3:23; Luke 5:36; 14:7); (4) ordinarily, in a more restricted sense, a comparison of earthly with heavenly things, “an earthly story with a heavenly meaning,” as in the parables of our Lord. Instruction by parables has been in use from the earliest times. A large portion of our Lord’s public teaching consisted of parables. He himself explains his reasons for this in his answer to the inquiry of the disciples, “Why speakest thou to them in parables?” (Matthew 13:13-15; Mark 4:11, 12; Luke 8:9, 10). He followed in so doing the rule of the divine procedures, as recorded in Matthew 13:13. The parables uttered by our Lord are all recorded in the synoptical (i.e., the first three) Gospels. The fourth Gospel contains no parable properly so called, although the illustration of the good shepherd (John 10:1-16) has all the essential features of a parable. (See List of Parables in Appendix.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GOAD (Hebrews malmad, only in Judges 3: 31), an instrument used by ploughmen for guiding their oxen. Shamgar slew six hundred Philistines with an ox-goad. “The goad is a formidable weapon. It is sometimes ten feet long, and has a sharp point. We could now see that the feat of Shamgar was not so very wonderful as some have been accustomed to think.” In 1 Samuel 13:21, a different Hebrew word is used, dorban, meaning something pointed. The expression (Acts 9:5, omitted in the R.V.), “It is hard for thee to kick against the pricks”, i.e., against the goad, was proverbial for unavailing resistance to superior power.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MERAB increase, the eldest of Saul’s two daughters (1 Samuel 14:49). She was betrothed to David after his victory over Goliath, but does not seem to have entered heartily into this arrangement (18:2, 17, 19). She was at length, however, married to Adriel of Abel-Meholah, a town in the Jordan valley, about 10 miles south of Bethshean, with whom the house of Saul maintained alliance. She had five sons, who were all put to death by the Gibeonites on the hill of Gibeah (2 Samuel 21:8).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MICHAL rivulet, or who as God?, the younger of Saul’s two daughters by his wife Ahinoam (1 Samuel 14:49, 50). “Attracted by the graces of his person and the gallantry of his conduct, she fell in love with David and became his wife” (18:20-28). She showed her affection for him by promoting his escape to Naioth when Saul sought his life (1 Samuel 19:12-17. Comp. Psalm 59. See TERAPHIM). After this she did not see David for many years. Meanwhile she was given in marriage to another man, Phalti or Phaltiel of Gallim (1 Samuel 25:44), but David afterwards formally reclaimed her as his lawful wife (2 Samuel 3:13-16). The relation between her and David soon after this was altered. They became alienated from each other. This happened on that memorable day when the ark was brought up in great triumph from its temporary resting-place to the Holy City. In David’s conduct on that occasion she saw nothing but a needless humiliation of the royal dignity (1 Chronicles 15:29). She remained childless, and thus the races of David and Saul were not mixed. In 2 Samuel 21:8 her name again occurs, but the name Merab should probably be here substituted for Michal (comp. 1 Samuel 18:19).

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: ABNER, ABNER, AHIMAAZ, AHINOAM, ARMIES.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ABNER father of light; i.e., “enlightening”, the son of Ner and uncle of Saul. He was commander-in-chief of Saul’s army (1 Samuel 14:50; 17:55; 20:25). He first introduced David to the court of Saul after the victory over Goliath (1 Samuel 17:57). After the death of Saul, David was made king over Judah, and reigned in Hebron. Among the other tribes there was a feeling of hostility to Judah; and Abner, at the head of Ephraim, fostered this hostility in the interest of the house of Saul, whose son Ish-bosheth he caused to be proclaimed king (2 Samuel 2:8). A state of war existed between these two kings. A battle fatal to Abner, who was the leader of Ish-boseth’s army, was fought with David’s army under Joab at Gibeon (2 Samuel 2:12). Abner, escaping from the field, was overtaken by Asahel, who was “light of foot as a wild roe,” the brother of Joab and Abishai, whom he thrust through with a back stroke of his spear (2 Samuel 2: 18-32). Being rebuked by Ish-bosheth for the impropriety of taking to wife Rizpah, who had been a concubine of King Saul, he found an excuse for going over to the side of David, whom he now professed to regard as anointed by the Lord to reign over all Israel. David received him favourably, and promised that he would have command of the armies. At this time Joab was absent from Hebron, but on his return he found what had happened. Abner had just left the city; but Joab by a stratagem recalled him, and meeting him at the gate of the city on his return, thrust him through with his sword (2 Samuel 3:27, 31-39; 4:12. Comp. 1 Kings 2:5, 32). David lamented in pathetic words the death of Abner, “Know ye not that there is a prince and a great man fallen this day in Israel?” (2 Samuel 3:33-38.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). AHIMAAZ brother of anger = irascible. (1.) The father Ahinoam, the wife of Saul (1 Samuel 14:50). (2.) The son and successor of Zadok in the office of high priest (1 Chronicles 6:8, 53). On the occasion of the revolt of Absalom he remained faithful to David, and was of service to him in conveying to him tidings of the proceedings of Absalom in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 15:24-37; 17:15-21). He was swift of foot, and was the first to carry to David tidings of the defeat of Absalom, although he refrained, from delicacy of feeling, from telling him of his death (2 Samuel 18:19-33).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). AHINOAM brother of pleasantness = pleasant. (1.) The daughter of Ahimaaz, and wife of Saul (1 Samuel 14:50). (2.) A Jezreelitess, the first wife of David (1 Samuel 25:43; 27:3). She was the mother of Amnon (2 Samuel 3:2). (See 1 Samuel 30:5, 18; 2 Samuel 2:2.)

↩ ◇ Note. The refused crown. Gideon’s formal refusal of dynastic kingship is one of the OT’s most explicit theological statements of pre-monarchic Yahwism: kingship over Israel belongs properly to Yahweh, and human kingship is a category mistake. The same theology drives Samuel’s warning in 1 Sam 8 ("they have rejected me from being king over them," 1 Sam 8:7). The chapter undermines Gideon’s refusal almost immediately: he asks for the gold of the Midianite spoil, makes an ephod of it, and "all Israel played the prostitute after it" (8:27). The pattern — verbal disavowal of kingship combined with practical accumulation of king-like prerogatives (concubines, 8:30; a son named Abimelech, "my father is king," 8:31) — exposes the gap between the theology articulated and the institution forming on the ground. Abimelech’s catastrophic kingship in ch 9 is the working-out of the contradiction.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CAMON full of stalks, a place (Judges 10:5) where Jair was buried. It has usually been supposed to have been a city of Gilead, on the east of Jordan. It is probably, however, the modern Tell-el-Kaimun, on the southern slopes of Carmel, the Jokneam of Carmel (Joshua 12:22; 1 Kings 4:12), since it is not at all unlikely that after he became judge, Jair might find it more convenient to live on the west side of Jordan; and that he was buried where he had lived.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ASHTORETH the moon goddess of the Phoenicians, representing the passive principle in nature, their principal female deity; frequently associated with the name of Baal, the sun-God, their chief male deity (Judges 10:6; 1 Samuel 7:4; 12:10). These names often occur in the plural (Ashtaroth, Baalim), probably as indicating either different statues or different modifications of the deities. This deity is spoken of as Ashtoreth of the Zidonians. She was the Ishtar of the Accadians and the Astarte of the Greeks (Jeremiah 44:17; 1 Kings 11:5, 33; 2 Kings 23:13). There was a temple of this goddess among the Philistines in the time of Saul (1 Samuel 31:10). Under the name of Ishtar, she was one of the great deities of the Assyrians. The Phoenicians called her Astarte. Solomon introduced the worship of this idol (1 Kings 11:33). Jezebel’s 400 priests were probably employed in its service (1 Kings 18:19). It was called the “queen of heaven” (Jeremiah 44:25).

↩ ◇ Note. The breaking of the cycle. The Judges narrative usually runs the Deuteronomistic cycle (apostasy → oppression → cry → deliverer → rest) without theological commentary on Yahweh’s motivation. Here, in 10:6–16, the cycle stalls: Israel cries; Yahweh refuses ("go cry to the gods you chose," 10:14); Israel removes the foreign gods and cries again; Yahweh "could no longer endure the misery of Israel" (10:16). The interlude is unique in the book — Yahweh is shown deliberating, refusing, and being moved by Israel’s repentance, not just running the program. The episode prepares for Jephthah’s deliverance in ch 11 and registers a theological development the rest of the book will not revisit: divine pity as the operative motive, not merely covenantal mechanism. Brueggemann reads the passage as one of the OT’s clearest portrayals of Yahweh’s pathos.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: AMMONITES, INSTANCES OF, EPHRAIM, MANASSEH, NAPHTALI, REUBEN, SIMEON, ZEBULUN, JEALOUSY.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SHIBBOLETH river, or an ear of corn. The tribes living on the east of Jordan, separated from their brethren on the west by the deep ravines and the rapid river, gradually came to adopt peculiar customs, and from mixing largely with the Moabites, Ishmaelites, and Ammonites to pronounce certain letters in such a manner as to distinguish them from the other tribes. Thus when the Ephraimites from the west invaded Gilead, and were defeated by the Gileadites under the leadership of Jephthah, and tried to escape by the “passages of the Jordan,” the Gileadites seized the fords and would allow none to pass who could not pronounce “shibboleth” with a strong aspirate. This the fugitives were unable to do. They said “sibboleth,” as the word was pronounced by the tribes on the west, and thus they were detected (Judges 12:1-6). Forty-two thousand were thus detected, and “Without reprieve, adjudged to death, For want of well-pronouncing shibboleth.”

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Shibbolet (שִׁבֹּלֶת). The Hebrew word means "ear of grain" or "stream"; its semantic content is irrelevant to the episode — the Gileadites are using it as a phonological test. Ephraimites pronounced the initial sibilant s (samekh-sound) where Gileadites used sh (shin-sound), an attested dialectal split between northern and Trans-Jordanian Hebrew confirmed by other inner-biblical evidence and by comparative Northwest Semitic data. The episode is the OT’s clearest single window on Hebrew dialect variation in the period of the Judges, and it has supplied English with the term shibboleth as a generic word for any pronunciation-test or in-group password used to identify outsiders. The forty-two thousand killed at the fords of the Jordan is hyperbolic, but the linguistic mechanism is precisely real.

↩ ◇ Note. Samson and the lion. The Spirit-empowered tearing of the lion with bare hands echoes both the Spirit-formula used of earlier judges (Othniel, Gideon, Jephthah) and the older Mesopotamian and Greek hero-pattern of lion-killing as a credentialing feat (Gilgamesh, Heracles). Samson’s portrayal is unique among the judges in its mythic-folkloric register — riddles, animal combat, supernatural strength, doomed love — and many scholars read the Samson narratives as preserving genuinely older heroic material absorbed into the deuteronomistic frame. The lion will return in 14:8 with the bees and honey, generating the riddle that drives the chapter. The verse also opens the Samson irony: he kills a lion barehanded by Spirit-power but does not "tell his father or his mother what he had done" — secrecy and concealment will define every subsequent stage of his relationships.

↩ ◇ Note. The jawbone weapon. The freshness of the jawbone matters: a dried bone would crumble; a fresh one (presumably from a recent carcass nearby) provides the dense material Samson needs. The detail and the resulting triumph-poem (15:16, "with the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps") are characteristic of the chapter’s folkloric register — a hero kills a thousand men with an improvised weapon and composes a punning couplet over the bodies (Hebrew ḥamor / ḥamoraim, "donkey / heap-of-heaps," exploits the consonance). The episode also names two springs (En-Hakkore, "spring of the caller," and Ramath-Lehi, "the height of the jawbone") in the etiological tradition the book regularly preserves. Samson’s own reflection in 15:18 — that he, the deliverer, will die of thirst and "fall into the hand of the uncircumcised" — registers the human limit of even his Spirit-empowered violence.

↩ ◇ Note. Micah’s shrine. The episode opens the book’s closing appendix (chs 17–21) — five chapters that abandon the deliverer-cycle to portray religious and political collapse. Micah’s shrine combines an Asherah-style image, an ephod (the priestly oracular vestment of legitimate cult, repurposed privately), teraphim (household idols), and a self-installed son as priest — a one-stop pseudo-Yahwistic compound entirely outside Levitical authority. The narrator’s subsequent installation of a wandering Levite as Micah’s priest (17:7–13) is meant to mark how completely the priestly office has decayed: a real Levite is for hire to a private idol shrine. The whole apparatus will be stolen by the Danite migrants in ch 18 and become the cult of the northern shrine at Dan — one of the OT’s pointed origin-stories for an institution it disapproves of (cf. 1 Kgs 12:29, where Jeroboam later sets up a calf at Dan). The genealogy of disorder begins here.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MAGIC The Jews seem early to have consulted the teraphim (q.v.) for oracular answers (Judges 18:5, 6; Zechariah 10:2). There is a remarkable illustration of this divining by teraphim in Ezekiel 21:19-22. We read also of the divining cup of Joseph (Genesis 44:5). The magicians of Egypt are frequently referred to in the history of the Exodus. Magic was an inherent part of the ancient Egyptian religion, and entered largely into their daily life. All magical arts were distinctly prohibited under penalty of death in the Mosaic law. The Jews were commanded not to learn the “abomination” of the people of the Promised Land (Leviticus 19:31; Deuteronomy 18:9-14). The history of Saul’s consulting the witch of Endor (1 Samuel 28:3-20) gives no warrant for attributing supernatural power to magicians. From the first the witch is here only a bystander. The practice of magic lingered among the people till after the Captivity, when they gradually abandoned it. It is not much referred to in the New Testament. The Magi mentioned in Matthew 2:1-12 were not magicians in the ordinary sense of the word. They belonged to a religious caste, the followers of Zoroaster, the astrologers of the East. Simon, a magician, was found by Philip at Samaria (Acts 8:9-24); and Paul and Barnabas encountered Elymas, a Jewish sorcerer, at Paphos (13:6-12). At Ephesus there was a great destruction of magical books (Acts 19:18, 19).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). LAISH a lion. (1.) A city of the Sidonians, in the extreme north of Palestine (Judges 18:7, 14); called also Leshem (Joshua 19:47) and Dan (Judges 18:7, 29; Jeremiah 8:16). It lay near the sources of the Jordan, about 4 miles from Paneas. The restless and warlike tribe of Dan (q.v.), looking out for larger possessions, invaded this country and took Laish with its territory. It is identified with the ruin Tell-el-Kady, “the mound of the judge,” to the north of the Waters of Merom (Joshua 11:5). (2.) A place mentioned in Isaiah 10:30. It has been supposed to be the modern el-Isawiyeh, about a mile north-east of Jerusalem. (3.) The father of Phalti (1 Samuel 25:44).

↩ ✧ Variant. The "captivity of the land." The verse names the priest of the Danite shrine as "Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Moses" — making Moses’ own grandson the founding priest of an idolatrous shrine. The MT has long been suspect: many manuscripts and the Vulgate read "the son of Manasseh" (Menasheh, מְנַשֶּׁה) — apparently a pious scribal alteration in which a suspended nun is inserted into "Moses" (Mosheh, מֹשֶׁה) to spare Moses’ name the embarrassment of an idolatrous descendant. The phenomenon (the "suspended nun" of Manasseh, nun teluyah) is preserved as a textual curiosity in many printed Hebrew Bibles and is one of the most famous examples of Masoretic discomfort with a Hebrew Bible reading. The "captivity of the land" most likely refers to the Assyrian destruction of Dan in 733/732 BCE under Tiglath-Pileser III — making the chapter’s composition or final editing post-733 BCE. The verse is one of the textbook cases of inner-biblical theological-political editing.

↩ ◇ Note. The Gibeah parallel. The chapter is a deliberate retelling of Gen 19 (Sodom): outsiders are received by an old sojourner, the men of the city demand to "know" the male guest, the host offers women instead, the demanded male is preserved while the woman is destroyed. The Hebrew vocabulary tracks the parallel point-for-point. The narrator’s argument is theologically devastating: an Israelite city, in the territory of Israel’s first king’s tribe (Benjamin, cf. 1 Sam 9–11), has become Sodom — the moral position of the Canaanites Israel was supposed to displace. The book’s closing refrain ("there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes," 21:25) is the editor’s diagnosis of how the inversion happened. Phyllis Trible’s reading of the chapter in Texts of Terror remains a major touchstone for feminist biblical scholarship — the concubine’s fate is the cost of all the political-theological calculations that frame her.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SLING With a sling and a stone David smote the Philistine giant (1 Samuel 17:40, 49). There were 700 Benjamites who were so skilled in its use that with the left hand they “could sling stones at a hair breadth, and not miss” (Judges 20:16; 1 Chronicles 12:2). It was used by the Israelites in war (2 Kings 3:25). (See ARMS.) The words in Proverbs 26:8, “As he that bindeth a stone in a sling,” etc. (Authorized Version), should rather, as in the Revised Version, be “As a bag of gems in a heap of stones,” etc.

↩ ◇ Note. The destruction of Benjamin. The civil war ends with near-extermination: the eleven tribes apply ḥerem (the ban — total destruction of cities, livestock, and inhabitants alike, the same vocabulary used of the Canaanite cities in Joshua) to Benjamin. The reversal is bitter and deliberate: the conquest-era ban, intended to clear the land of Canaanite practice, is now applied by Israel to one of its own tribes for behaving like Canaanites. Six hundred Benjaminite men survive (20:47), and the next chapter strains to find them wives — including the kidnapping of dancing girls at Shiloh (21:21) — to prevent the tribe’s extinction. The chapter that produced Israel’s first king (Saul, of Benjamin) had to be saved from itself; the bookends of pre-monarchic Israel and the monarchy meet in a tribe nearly destroyed for the violation that opens chs 19–21.

↩ ◇ Note. The dance at Shiloh. The annual women’s dance at Shiloh — likely the harvest festival or a related agricultural celebration — preserves a memory of pre-monarchic Israelite ritual life with female participation and outdoor cultic celebration of a kind that fades from later representations. The book’s closing scene weaponizes this ritual: Benjaminite survivors lie in wait among the vineyards and seize wives at the festival, with the elders’ explicit advance approval. The irony is total — the book opened with the conquest of Canaan and closes with Israelite men kidnapping Israelite women at a Yahweh-festival to repopulate a tribe nearly exterminated for kidnapping a woman. The final verse (21:25, "in those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes") is the editor’s judgment on the entire arc, and the Shiloh kidnapping is the final image he wants the reader to carry into the books of Samuel.

↩ ◇ Note. The minor judges and the donkey colts. Jair’s thirty sons riding thirty donkey colts and ruling thirty cities (similar to Ibzan’s thirty sons and thirty daughters in 12:9 and Abdon’s forty sons on seventy donkey colts in 12:14) preserves a glimpse of an alternate model of pre-monarchic Israelite leadership: clan-patriarchs whose authority was hereditary, regionally distributed, and signaled by visible markers of household wealth (sons, daughters, donkeys, fortified towns). The repeated pattern in the "minor judges" sections (10:1–5, 12:8–15) suggests a period of relative stability between the spectacular deliverer-narratives — kingship-like authority in functional terms without the title or theology. Donkey-riding as a marker of elite status (rather than horseback) is consistent with pre-monarchic Israelite practice: cf. Zech 9:9 ("your king comes… humble and riding on a donkey"), preserving the older association of donkey-riding with legitimate non-imperial rule. The minor judges are the structural background against which the major figures (Jephthah, Samson) operate.

↩ ◇ Note. The Ephraimite quarrel. Ephraim’s grievance — that they were not summoned to fight Ammon — is identical in form to their earlier quarrel with Gideon (8:1–3), but where Gideon defused the complaint with a soft answer, Jephthah escalates and crushes them at the Jordan fords. The pattern reveals a recurrent structural tension in pre-monarchic Israel: Ephraim, the largest northern tribe, held an honor-claim to inclusion in any major tribal-coalition action and treated exclusion as cause for civil war. The same tension drives the later split of the kingdom under Jeroboam I (1 Kgs 12), an Ephraimite, whose legitimacy claim in the north rests on Ephraim’s historic resentment of southern-led tribal coalitions. Jephthah’s ferocity here, combined with Gideon’s tact earlier, frames the long-running political problem the eventual monarchy will inherit: the inability of the tribal confederation to manage Ephraim’s honor-politics is the deep structural failure the book diagnoses.

↩ ◇ Note. Laish’s vulnerability. The Danite spies report Laish as ideal for conquest precisely because it is peaceful: isolated from Sidon, undefended, "quiet and secure," with "no one in the land possessing authority." The Hebrew narrator’s language is theologically unmistakable — these are the Sodom virtues (Gen 19) the book has just been recapitulating elsewhere. The Danite migration is the negative inverse of the Joshua-era conquest: where Joshua’s armies were sent to dispossess hostile Canaanite city-states under Yahweh’s explicit warrant, the Danites of Judges 18 attack a peaceful unrelated city of their own initiative because the original Danite tribal allotment (the coastal plain south of Joppa, Josh 19:40–48) had been crowded out by Philistine pressure. The chapter shows tribal Israel improvising migrations and conquests outside any covenantal frame — the same pattern that produces the cult-shrine theft in 18:14–20. The verse marks the moral floor of the book’s closing chapters before the Gibeah outrage of ch 19.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). OREB , THE ROCK OF the place where Gideon slew Oreb after the defeat of the Midianites (Judges 7:25; Isaiah 10:26). It was probably the place now called Orbo, on the east of Jordan, near Bethshean.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ZEEB the wolf, one of the two leaders of the great Midianite host which invaded Israel and was utterly routed by Gideon. The division of that host, which attempted to escape across the Jordan, under Oreb and Zeeb, was overtaken by the Ephraimites, who, in a great battle, completely vanquished them, their leaders being taken and slain (Judges 7:25; Psalm 83:11; Isaiah 10:26).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). TOMBS of the Hebrews were generally excavated in the solid rock, or were natural caves. Mention is made of such tombs in Judges 8:32; 2 Samuel 2:32; 2 Kings 9:28; 23:30. They were sometimes made in gardens (2 Kings 21:26; 23:16; Matthew 27:60). They are found in great numbers in and around Jerusalem and all over the land. They were sometimes whitewashed (Matthew 23:27, 29). The body of Jesus was laid in Joseph’s new rock-hewn tomb, in a garden near to Calvary. All evidence is in favour of the opinion that this tomb was somewhere near the Damascus gate, and outside the city, and cannot be identified with the so-called “holy sepulchre.” The mouth of such rocky tombs was usually closed by a large stone (Hebrews golal), which could only be removed by the united efforts of several men (Matthew 28:2; comp. John 11:39). (See GOLGOTHA.)

In 9:46 he is called simply “the God Berith.” The name denotes the God of the covenant into which the Israelites entered with the Canaanites, contrary to the command of Jehovah (Exodus 34:12), when they began to fall away to the worship of idols.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ABEL-CHERAMIM (Judges 11:33, R.V.; A. V., “plain of the vineyards”), a village of the Ammonites, whither Jephthah pursued their forces.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MINNITH distribution, an Ammonitish town (Judges 11:33) from which wheat was exported to Tyre (Ezekiel 27:17). It was probably somewhere in the Mishor or table-land on the east of Jordan. There is a gentle valley running for about 4 miles east of Dhiban called Kurm Dhiban, “the vineyards of Dibon.” Tristram supposes that this may be the “vineyards” mentioned in Judges (l.c.).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PLAIN (1.) Hebrews ‘abel (Judges 11:33), a “grassy plain” or “meadow.” Instead of “plains of the vineyards,” as in the Authorized Version, the Revised Version has “Abel-cheramim” (q.v.), comp. Judges 11:22; 2 Chronicles 16:4. (2.) Hebrews ‘elon (Genesis 12:6; 13:18; 14:13; 18:1; Deuteronomy 11:30; Judges 9:6), more correctly “oak,” as in the Revised Version; margin, “terebinth.” (3.) Hebrews bik’ah (Genesis 11:2; Nehemiah 6:2; Ezekiel 3:23; Daniel 3:1), properly a valley, as rendered in Isaiah 40:4, a broad plain between mountains. In Amos 1:5 the margin of Authorized Version has “Bikathaven.” (4.) Hebrews kikar, “the circle,” used only of the Ghor, or the low ground along the Jordan (Genesis 13:10-12; 19:17, 25, 28, 29; Deuteronomy 34:3; 2 Samuel 18:23; 1 Kings 7:46; 2 Chronicles 4:17; Nehemiah 3:22; 12:28), the floor of the valley through which it flows. This name is applied to the Jordan valley as far north as Succoth. (5.) Hebrews mishor, “level ground,” smooth, grassy table-land (Deuteronomy 3:10; 4:43; Joshua 13:9, 16, 17, 21; 20:8; Jeremiah 48:21), an expanse of rolling downs without rock or stone. In these passages, with the article prefixed, it denotes the plain in the tribe of Reuben. In 2 Chronicles 26:10 the plain of Judah is meant. Jerusalem is called “the rock of the plain” in Jeremiah 21:13, because the hills on which it is built rise high above the plain. (6.) Hebrews ‘arabah, the valley from the Sea of Galilee southward to the Dead Sea (the “sea of the plain,” 2 Kings 14:25; Deuteronomy 1:1; 2:8), a distance of about 70 miles. It is called by the modern Arabs the Ghor. This Hebrew name is found in Authorized Version (Joshua 18:18), and is uniformly used in the Revised Version. Down through the centre of this plain is a ravine, from 200 to 300 yards wide, and from 50 to 100 feet deep, through which the Jordan flows in a winding course. This ravine is called the “lower plain.” The name Arabah is also applied to the whole Jordan valley from Mount Hermon to the eastern branch of the Red Sea, a distance of about 200 miles, as well as to that portion of the valley which stretches from the Sea of Galilee to the same branch of the Red Sea, i.e., to the Gulf of Akabah about 100 miles in all. (7.) Hebrews shephelah, “low ground,” “low hill-land,” rendered “vale” or “valley” in Authorized Version (Joshua 9:1; 10:40; 11:2; 12:8; Judges 1:9; 1 Kings 10:27). In Authorized Version (1 Chronicles 27:28; 2 Chronicles 26:10) it is also rendered “low country.” In Jeremiah 17:26, Obad. 1:19, Zechariah 7:7, “plain.” The Revised Version renders it uniformly “low land.” When it is preceded by the article, as in Deuteronomy 1:7, Joshua 11:16; 15:33, Jeremiah 32:44; 33:13, Zechariah 7:7, “the shephelah,” it denotes the plain along the Mediterranean from Joppa to Gaza, “the plain of the Philistines.” (See VALLEY.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ABDON servile. (1.) The son of Hillel, a Pirathonite, the tenth judge of Israel (Judges 12:13-15). He is probably the Bedan of 1 Samuel 12:11. (2.) The first-born of Gibeon of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:30; 9:36). (3.) The son of Micah, one of those whom Josiah sent to the prophetess Huldah to ascertain from her the meaning of the recently discovered book of the law (2 Chronicles 34:20). He is called Achbor in 2 Kings 22:12. (4.) One of the “sons” of Shashak (1 Chronicles 8:23). This is the name also of a Levitical town of the Gershonites, in the tribe of Asher (Joshua 21:30; 1 Chronicles 6:74). The ruins of Abdeh, some 8 miles north-east of Accho, probably mark its site.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HILLEL praising, a Pirathonite, father of the judge Abdon (Judges 12:13, 15).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PIRATHONITE (1.) Abdon, the son of Hillel, so called, Judges 12:13, 15. (2.) Benaiah the Ephraimite (2 Samuel 23:30), one of David’s thirty heroes.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). JONATHAN whom Jehovah gave, the name of fifteen or more persons that are mentioned in Scripture. The chief of these are, (1.) A Levite descended from Gershom (Judges 18:30). His history is recorded in 17:7-13 and 18:30. The Rabbins changed this name into Manasseh “to screen the memory of the great lawgiver from the stain of having so unworthy an apostate among his near descendants.” He became priest of the idol image at Dan, and this office continued in his family till the Captivity. (2.) The eldest son of king Saul, and the bosom friend of David. He is first mentioned when he was about thirty years of age, some time after his father’s accession to the throne (1 Samuel 13:2). Like his father, he was a man of great strength and activity (2 Samuel 1:23), and excelled in archery and slinging (1 Chronicles 12:2;2 Samuel 1:22). The affection that evidently subsisted between him and his father was interrupted by the growth of Saul’s insanity. At length, “in fierce anger,” he left his father’s presence and cast in his lot with the cause of David (1 Samuel 20:34). After an eventful career, interwoven to a great extent with that of David, he fell, along with his father and his two brothers, on the fatal field of Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:2, 8). He was first buried at Jabesh-gilead, but his remains were afterwards removed with those of his father to Zelah, in Benjamin (2 Samuel 21:12-14). His death was the occasion of David’s famous elegy of “the Song of the Bow” (2 Samuel 1:17-27). He left one son five years old, Merib-baal, or Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 4:4; comp. 1 Chronicles 8:34). (3.) Son of the high priest Abiathar, and one who adhered to David at the time of Absalom’s rebellion (2 Samuel 15:27, 36). He is the last descendant of Eli of whom there is any record. (4.) Son of Shammah, and David’s nephew, and also one of his chief warriors (2 Samuel 21:21). He slew a giant in Gath.

The Book of Judges 7:1.

Then Jerubbaal, who [is] Gideon, and all the people that [were] with him, rose up early, and pitched beside the well of Harod: so that the host of the Midianites were on the north side of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

וַיַּשְׁכֵּ֨ם יְרֻבַּ֜עַל ה֣וּא גִדְע֗וֹן וְכָל־הָעָם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אִתּ֔וֹ וַֽיַּחֲנ֖וּ עַל־עֵ֣ין חֲרֹ֑ד וּמַחֲנֵ֤ה מִדְיָן֙ הָיָה־ל֣וֹ מִצָּפ֔וֹן מִגִּבְעַ֥ת הַמּוֹרֶ֖ה בָּעֵֽמֶק׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

Καὶ ὤρθρισεν Ἰαρβάλ, αὐτός ἐστιν Γεδεών, καὶ πᾶς ὁ λαὸς μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ, καὶ παρενέβαλον ἐπὶ πηγὴν Ἀράδ· καὶ παρεμβολὴ Μαδιὰμ ἦν αὐτῷ ἀπὸ βορρᾶ ἀπὸ Γαβααθαμωρὰ ἐν κοιλάδι.

Douay-Rheims

Then Jerobaal, who is the same as Gedeon, rising up early and all the people with him, came to the fountain that is called Harad. Now the camp of Madian was in the valley on the north side of the high hill.

JPS (1917)

Then Jerubbaal, who is Gideon, and all the people that were with him, rose up early, and pitched beside En-harod; and the camp of Midian was on the north side of them, by Gibeath-moreh, in the valley.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Igitur Jerobaal qui et Gedeon, de nocte consurgens, et omnis populus cum eo, venit ad fontem qui vocatur Harad. Erant autem castra Madian in valle ad septentrionalem plagam collis excelsi.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

فَبَكَّرَ يَرُبَّعْلُ، أَيْ جِدْعُونُ، وَكُلُّ ٱلشَّعْبِ ٱلَّذِي مَعَهُ وَنَزَلُوا عَلَى عَيْنِ حَرُودَ. وَكَانَ جَيْشُ ٱلْمِدْيَانِيِّينَ شِمَالِيَّهُمْ عِنْدَ تَلِّ مُورَةَ فِي ٱلْوَادِي.

↩

The Book of Judges 7:2.

And the LORD said unto Gideon, The people that [are] with thee [are] too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ אֶל־גִּדְע֔וֹן רַ֗ב הָעָם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אִתָּ֔ךְ מִתִּתִּ֥י אֶת־מִדְיָ֖ן בְּיָדָ֑ם פֶּן־יִתְפָּאֵ֨ר עָלַ֤י יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר יָדִ֖י הוֹשִׁ֥יעָה לִּֽי׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

καὶ εἶπεν Κύριος πρὸς Γεδεών Πολὺς ὁ λαὸς ὁ μετὰ σοῦ ὥστε μὴ παραδοῦναί με τὴν Μαδιὰμ ἐν χειρὶ αὐτῶν, μή ποτε καυχήσηται Ἰσραὴλ ἐπ᾽ ἐμὲ λέγων Ἡ χείρ μου ἔσωσέν με.

Douay-Rheims

And the Lord said to Gedeon: The people that are with thee are many, and Madian shall not be delivered into their hands: lest Israel should glory against me, and say: I was delivered by my own strength.

JPS (1917)

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Arabic (Van Dyck)

وَقَالَ ٱلرَّبُّ لِجِدْعُونَ: «إِنَّ ٱلشَّعْبَ ٱلَّذِي مَعَكَ كَثِيرٌ عَلَيَّ لِأَدْفَعَ ٱلْمِدْيَانِيِّينَ بِيَدِهِمْ، لِئَلَّا يَفْتَخِرَ عَلَيَّ إِسْرَائِيلُ قَائِلًا: يَدِي خَلَّصَتْنِي.

The Book of Judges 7:3.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

וְעַתָּ֗ה קְרָ֨א נָ֜א בְּאָזְנֵ֤י הָעָם֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר מִֽי־יָרֵ֣א וְחָרֵ֔ד יָשֹׁ֥ב וְיִצְפֹּ֖ר מֵהַ֣ר הַגִּלְעָ֑ד וַיָּ֣שָׁב מִן־הָעָ֗ם עֶשְׂרִ֤ים וּשְׁנַ֨יִם֙ אֶ֔לֶף וַעֲשֶׂ֥רֶת אֲלָפִ֖ים נִשְׁאָֽרוּ׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

Douay-Rheims

Speak to the people, and proclaim in the hearing of all, I Whosoever is fearful and timorous, let him return. So two and twenty thousand men went away from mount Galaad and returned home, and only ten thousand remained.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Arabic (Van Dyck)

وَٱلْآنَ نَادِ فِي آذَانِ ٱلشَّعْبِ قَائِلًا: مَنْ كَانَ خَائِفًا وَمُرْتَعِدًا فَلْيَرْجِعْ وَيَنْصَرِفْ مِنْ جَبَلِ جِلْعَادَ». فَرَجَعَ مِنَ ٱلشَّعْبِ ٱثْنَانِ وَعِشْرُونَ أَلْفًا. وَبَقِيَ عَشَرَةُ آلَافٍ.

The Book of Judges 7:4.

And the LORD said unto Gideon, The people [are] yet [too] many; bring them down unto the water, and I will try them for thee there: and it shall be, [that] of whom I say unto thee, This shall go with thee, the same shall go with thee; and of whomsoever I say unto thee, This shall not go with thee, the same shall not go.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוָ֜ה אֶל־גִּדְע֗וֹן עוֹד֮ הָעָ֣ם רָב֒ הוֹרֵ֤ד אוֹתָם֙ אֶל־הַמַּ֔יִם וְאֶצְרְפֶ֥נּוּ לְךָ֖ שָׁ֑ם וְהָיָ֡ה אֲשֶׁר֩ אֹמַ֨ר אֵלֶ֜יךָ זֶ֣ה ׀ יֵלֵ֣ךְ אִתָּ֗ךְ ה֚וּא יֵלֵ֣ךְ אִתָּ֔ךְ וְכֹ֨ל אֲשֶׁר־אֹמַ֜ר אֵלֶ֗יךָ זֶ֚ה לֹא־יֵלֵ֣ךְ עִמָּ֔ךְ ה֖וּא לֹ֥א יֵלֵֽךְ׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

καὶ εἶπεν Κύριος πρὸς Γεδεών Ἔτι ὁ λαὸς πολύς· κατένεγκον αὐτοὺς πρὸς τὸ ὕδωρ, καὶ ἐκκαθαρῶ σοι αὐτὸν ἐκεῖ· καὶ ἔσται ὃν ἐὰν εἴπω πρὸς σέ Οὗτος πορεύσεται σὺν σοί, αὐτὸς πορεύσεται σὺν σοί· καὶ πᾶς ὃν ἐὰν εἴπω πρὸς σέ Οὗτος οὐ πορεύσεται μετὰ σοῦ, αὐτὸς οὐ πορεύσεται μετὰ σοῦ.

Douay-Rheims

And the Lord said to Gedeon: The people are still too many, bring them to the waters, and there I will try them: and of whom I shall say to thee, This shall go with thee, let him go: whom I shall forbid to go, let him return.

JPS (1917)

And the LORD said unto Gideon: 'The people are yet too many; bring them down unto the water, and I will try them for thee there; and it shall be, that of whom I say to thee: This shall go with thee, the same shall go with thee; and of whomsoever I say unto thee: This shall not go with thee, the same shall not go.'

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Dixitque Dominus ad Gedeon: Adhuc populus multus est: duc eos ad aquas et ibi probabo illos: et de quo dixero tibi ut tecum vadat, ipse pergat; quem ire prohibuero, revertatur.

The Book of Judges 7:5.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

And the LORD said unto Gideon, By the three hundred men that lapped will I save you, and deliver the Midianites into thine hand: and let all the [other] people go every man unto his place.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוָ֜ה אֶל־גִּדְע֗וֹן בִּשְׁלֹשׁ֩ מֵא֨וֹת הָאִ֤ישׁ הַֽמֲלַקְקִים֙ אוֹשִׁ֣יעַ אֶתְכֶ֔ם וְנָתַתִּ֥י אֶת־מִדְיָ֖ן בְּיָדֶ֑ךָ וְכָל־הָעָ֔ם יֵלְכ֖וּ אִ֥ישׁ לִמְקֹמֽוֹ׃

فَقَالُوا: «وَمَا هُوَ قُرْبَانُ ٱلْإِثْمِ ٱلَّذِي نَرُدُّهُ لَهُ؟» فَقَالُوا: «حَسَبَ عَدَدِ أَقْطَابِ ٱلْفِلِسْطِينِيِّينَ: خَمْسَةَ بَوَاسِيرَ مِنْ ذَهَبٍ، وَخَمْسَةَ فِيرَانٍ مِنْ ذَهَبٍ. لِأَنَّ ٱلضَّرْبَةَ وَاحِدَةٌ عَلَيْكُمْ جَمِيعًا وَعَلَى أَقْطَابِكُمْ.

↩

The First Book of Samuel 6:5.

Wherefore ye shall make images of your emerods, and images of your mice that mar the land; and ye shall give glory unto the God of Israel: peradventure he will lighten his hand from off you, and from off your gods, and from off your land.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

καὶ μῦς χρυσοῦς ὁμοίωμα τῶν μυῶν ὑμῶν τῶν διαφθειρόντων τὴν γῆν. καὶ δώσετε τῷ κυρίῳ δόξαν, ὅπως κουφίσῃ τὴν χεῖρα αὐτοῦ ἀφ᾽ ὑμῶν καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν θεῶν ὑμῶν καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ὑμῶν.

Douay-Rheims

According to the number of the provinces of the Philistines you shall make five golden emerods, and five golden mice: for the same plague hath been upon you all, and upon your lords. And you shall make the likeness of your emerods, and the likeness of the mice that have destroyed the land, and you shall give glory to the God of Israel: to see if he will take off his hand from you, and from your gods, and from your land.

JPS (1917)

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Juxta numerum provinciarum Philisthinorum quinque anos aureos facietis, et quinque mures aureos: quia plaga una fuit omnibus vobis, et satrapis vestris. Facietisque similitudines anorum vestrorum, et similitudines murium, qui demoliti sunt terram: et dabitis Deo Israël gloriam, si forte relevet manum suam a vobis, et a diis vestris, et a terra vestra.
